title: Course Outline
text:
AKA Intermediate Dynamics (ME 4730/5730 on ruina.org).
Instructor: Prof. Andy Ruina


The course emphasizes the classical dynamics of single- and multi-degree-of-freedom systems made up of particles, rigid-objects in 2 and 3 special dimensions. The course emphasizes finding equations of motion, solving them analytically (if possible) and numerically; and graphical presentation of solutions, including animations and simulations.
This will be taught in three different ways: 1. Newton Euler – minimal coordinates 2. Newton Euler – maximal coordinates 3. Lagrangian




The student will be able to find the governing equations of motion for a variety of dynamic mechanical systems consisting of particles and rigid objects that might interact with various standard connections (e.g., strings, springs, hinges, rolling, surface sliding) and forces (e.g., gravity, friction, fluid drag).
The student will be able to solve the simple cases by hand, solve the more complex cases with numerical integration (Matlab), graphically represent the results, including animations.
The student will be able to check the reasonableness of the results using extreme cases and Laws of Conservation (momentum, angular momentum and energy).
The student will be able to use principles of Lagrangian mechanics to develop the same governing equations as above for simple conservative systems.
The student will be able to formulate, setup, numerically solve, and interpret the equations and solutions of a 3D rigid object rotating in space.





A book on Dynamics at a higher level than Ruina and Pratap, e.g. Greenwood.
Dennis Bernstein’s online book. Bernstein is compulsive about clear notation for reference frames etc. (Write to author, no public link.)
Murray, Li and Sastry, A Matematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation, 1994. Another rather formal approach.
Dave Baraff’s Physically based modeling notes.
Dave Block’s out-of-print book on tensors “A vector is a vector.” (H.D. Block, Introduction to tensor analysis (pdf))
Savransky’s Matlab stuff for rotations.




The grading is divided into:

Homework: 50%

To be submitted weekly, late submissions will be discarded towards the student’s grading.
Best 12/15 homeworks will be considers i.e. you can drop 3 homeworks.
Record how much time you spend on your homeworks.
Homeworks are due Tuesday 11 PM

Viva 1: 25%

30-minute viva based entirely on your homework. If the student has done all the homework, watched the lectures, and spent at least their 4.5 hours/week on the course, they will do well.

Viva 2: 25%

30-minute viva based entirely on your homework. If the student has done all the homework, watched the lectures, and spent at least their 4.5 hours/week on the course, they will do well.

Attendance: %TBD

Attendance for our weekly discussion.





For Plaksha 2026 students:
Students should self police each other and make sure they are watching the lectures and putting in the required number of hours into their homework, every week.
You are expected to put in 2.5 hours/credit/week into this course. That is 7.5 hours of effort per week, plus we have missed a week so it’s more about 8 hours/week, Subtracting the 2 hours of lectures and an hour of discussion, that leaves you with 4.5 hours + a little bit more to do your homeworks.
Each person should evaluate someone else’s claims on effort in homeworks, and whether they have watched the lectures or not.
Meher Sidhu is appointed as the class’ police officer but this is on all of you.



The lecture list is maintained live on the Lectures page, along with the recording and lecture-note links for each one. Students are expected to watch at least two lectures per week.

title: About
text:
This is the course site for Dynamics & Simulation (AKA Intermediate Dynamics, ME 4730/5730), taught by Prof. Andy Ruina at Plaksha University, reusing the Cornell lecture recordings.
The site is a static Quarto website. Everything on the Lectures and Homework pages is generated at build time from a single spreadsheet plus the folders of PDFs — there is no database and no backend.

title: About
text:
How to update this site
Adding a year of videos, a new set of lecture notes, or a new set of solutions is a spreadsheet + folder change. It should never need a code change.

1. Edit Dynamics&Sim-MasterSheet.xlsx
This file is the source of truth. Two sheets:
Lectures — one row per lecture.







Column
What it does




Lec No., Name of Lecture
Fixed identity columns.


Link (YYYY)
A set of video links. The label shown on the site is whatever is inside the parentheses. Add a whole new year by adding a new column, e.g. Link (2027). A cell may hold more than one URL.


Any other column
A notes set. The header must match a folder name under Notes/ exactly. Each cell holds the note number(s) covering that lecture.



Notes cells accept 7, 16, 17, or 03, 04 -> some commentary (the trailing commentary becomes a tooltip). Leave a cell blank for “no notes”.
Homeworks — one row per problem.







Column
What it does




Homework No. (Plaksha Doc)
Fixed identity column. Must match the problem numbering inside the combined homework PDF.


Done Last Time (...)
Usage history — y or n. Add another column, e.g. Done Last Time (2027 Plaksha), to track another offering.


Any other column
A solutions set. The header must match a folder name under Homework/ exactly. Each cell holds the solution code, e.g. Q01.









Important



Excel sometimes autocorrects an entry like 9, 10 into a date. If it does, format the cell as Text and retype the value — otherwise the build will warn and skip that cell.




2. Add the matching folder
For a new notes or solutions set, create a folder under Notes/ or Homework/ named exactly like the new column header, and drop the files in it.

Notes files are matched by their leading number: 7. Whatever.pdf, 07 Whatever.pdf and Lecture 07 Whatever.pdf all resolve to note 7. One file can cover several notes (Lecture 09 10 ....pdf).
Solution files are matched by their code prefix: Q01...pdf. A solution may live in a same-named subfolder alongside supporting .m/.png files, which get listed with it.
A filename or folder containing any of the keywords below is flagged with a ⚠ “not instructor-reviewed” badge. Punctuation and capitalisation are ignored when matching, so Not Approved and NotApproved both count. Edit UNAPPROVED_KEYWORDS at the top of scripts/build_data.py to change the list — this page reads it from there, so it cannot go stale:
NotApproved, NotYetApproved, NotYetFinallyApproved, NonFinalized, NotAndyApproved, NotAndyAproved, DamnGood
Anything left over in a solutions folder that no row references is still published, under “Other materials” on the Homework page.



3. Render locally to check
pip install -r requirements.txt
quarto render
The pre-render step regenerates _data/ and prints warnings for anything it could not resolve — an unparseable cell, a missing note file, a solution code with no matching PDF. Read those warnings; they are how you catch typos.
Use quarto preview for a live-reloading local copy.


4. Commit and push
git add -A && git commit -m "Update course materials" && git push
GitHub Actions rebuilds and redeploys the site automatically on every push to main.

title: About
text:
How it fits together

scripts/build_data.py — pre-render step. Reads the spreadsheet, scans Notes/ and Homework/, resolves every reference to a real file, works out which page of the combined PDF each problem starts on, and writes JSON into _data/.
scripts/coursesite.py — small helpers the pages use to turn that JSON into links and badges.
lectures.qmd / homework.qmd — read the JSON and render it with itables, which gives client-side sorting, searching and paging on a fully static page.
_data/ and files/ are generated on every render and are not checked in.

The site is intentionally public — there is no login.
